title: Charge moves; neutral objects respond
question: If both objects start neutral, can rubbing create net charge?
explanation: Rubbing moves electrons from one object to the other; it does not create charge. A positive electron deficit on one object exactly matches the negative excess elsewhere. A nearby neutral sample can rearrange its charges while its total charge stays zero.
limits: Counted charges and displacements are enlarged. Polarisation force is a qualitative proxy, not a molecular simulation.

title: Inside a conducting shell
question: Does a metal shell merely weaken the external electric field?
explanation: Mobile electrons in the metal rearrange until their field cancels the applied field inside the empty cavity. Compare the external field with the induced field, then add them. The transparent inspection view does not make a hole in the shell.
limits: Analytic conducting sphere in a uniform static field. The cutaway is a view, not a physical opening; this does not model radio-frequency shielding.

title: Slow electrons, fast signal
question: Must an electron travel from the battery to the LED before the LED responds?
explanation: The wire already contains mobile electrons all along its length. A change in the electric field reaches distant parts of the circuit quickly, while each electron drifts only a tiny distance. The two clocks separate those very different speeds.
limits: Illustrative 1 m wire, signal speed 10^8 m/s and chosen drift speed 0.1 mm/s; the two clocks have separate labelled scales.

title: Find the dark LED
question: Can a battery show its normal voltage and still fail under load?
explanation: Current must pass through the battery’s internal resistance as well as the LED and its resistor. More current causes a larger voltage drop inside the battery, so a battery can show its normal voltage without a load yet supply much less current when connected. The graph’s dot is where the source and load agree on one current and terminal voltage.
limits: Illustrative exponential I–V with nVt=0.08 V, calibrated to 20 mA at red 2.0 V / white 3.3 V; temperature, leakage, reverse breakdown and component specifications omitted.

title: Measure two branches
question: Do unequal parallel branches have equal current or equal voltage?
explanation: Parallel branches touch the same two junctions, so they share the same voltage difference. The branch with greater resistance carries less current. In series there is only one path, so both loads carry the same current even when their voltage drops differ.
limits: Ideal resistors and fixed 2 V LED drops in this topology lesson; these are separate from the nonlinear diagnostic model.

title: A fault in the case
question: Does a small current leaking to earth look like an overload?
explanation: Current leaving by live should return by neutral. A separate route to earth makes those currents unequal, so the residual-current device opens the switch. A balanced overload can have no such imbalance yet still require an overcurrent breaker.
limits: Prescribed prospective fault current, ideal latched 30 mA imbalance / 16 A overload comparisons, no real trip timing or body-resistance prediction; all routes are virtual.

title: Domains inside a magnet
question: When a magnet is cut, can one half contain only a north pole?
explanation: Neighbouring magnetic moments form domains whose different directions can largely cancel. An applied field favours some orientations, moving domain walls and turning moments. Cutting the material does not split those moments into isolated north and south poles: each piece remains a complete magnet.
limits: Schematic domains: field-dependent orientation and favourable-region growth, not a quantitative hysteresis or atomic-spin model.

title: A compass that can dip
question: Does a compass reveal the complete direction of Earth’s field?
explanation: A freely suspended needle can follow the full sloping magnetic field. Holding it level prevents vertical motion, so it can reveal only the horizontal projection. Rotating the device changes its measured components without rotating the world field.
limits: Centred ideal dipole, not a local geomagnetic forecast. Latitude controls the ideal dip, which differs from measured Mumbai values.

title: Add wire and Earth fields
question: Will reversing the wire current turn a compass exactly 180 degrees?
explanation: A compass follows the sum of all magnetic fields at its location. The wire’s field circles the wire and reverses with the current, while the northward background remains. Reversing only the wire therefore need not reverse the whole resultant field.
limits: Long straight wire, 38.4 microtesla horizontal background. The tram preset treats one distant current and omits the return conductor. Coil contributions use the on-axis Biot–Savart field of circular loops of 1 cm radius, spaced 1 mm apart. The centre probe is fixed in that mode; field-arrow scales are printed separately.

title: Step inside a motor
question: Why must the current reverse every half-turn?
explanation: Opposite sides of the coil carry opposite currents and feel opposite sideways forces, producing a turning effect. After half a turn, unchanged current would reverse that turning effect. The split ring swaps the current direction so the turning effect keeps the same sense.
limits: Uniform 0.5 T field, 10 turns of 0.04 m² area. Rotor inertia 0.08 kg·m² and damping 0.35 s^-1 are chosen model values; ideal instantaneous commutation. Holding freezes the rotor for inspection; open circuit removes electrical torque while a moving rotor coasts. Back emf is omitted.

title: Turn a generator
question: Does the largest flux always mean the largest induced voltage?
explanation: As the coil turns, the amount of magnetic field passing through it changes; this amount is called flux. Induced voltage follows how quickly the flux changes. At a maximum or minimum flux, the change is momentarily zero, so the voltage is zero even though the flux is large.
limits: Uniform field, ideal coil; mechanical rotation is supplied externally. Loading and self-inductance are omitted.

title: Two coils, one changing field
question: Can a steady direct current keep inducing voltage in a second coil?
explanation: A changing magnetic field in the shared core produces a voltage around each coil. More turns add more induced voltage, giving the turns ratio. Steady direct current leaves a steady field after switching, so it gives no sustained secondary voltage.
limits: AC control is RMS voltage, with an ideal resistive secondary load and no core losses/saturation. Separate steady DC comparison assumes 10 Ω primary winding resistance and schematic stored flux; switching transient omitted.

title: Two fields across a gap
question: Does either field point along the wave’s travel direction?
explanation: At a fixed point the electric and magnetic fields change together. Both point across the direction of travel, at right angles to one another. The moving curves show a travelling pattern of field values, not material moving along the curves.
limits: Plane wave; amplitudes use independent diagram scales. Wavelength spans are normalised and the animation is enormously slowed.

title: Earth turns beneath the sky
question: Which way must Earth turn for stars to seem to move west?
explanation: Earth turns eastward beneath the distant Sun and stars. The same surface observer moves between the lit and dark hemispheres, while the sky appears to move the other way. The local-horizon view describes those same directions from the observer’s turning frame.
limits: Ideal sphere and distant Sun; solar time, not Mumbai civil time. Star coordinates are illustrative.

title: Tilt, sunlight and daylight
question: If tilt is zero but the orbit remains, do the seasons remain?
explanation: A hemisphere tilted toward the Sun receives higher-angle sunlight over a smaller footprint and has longer daylight. The opposite hemisphere receives lower-angle sunlight and shorter days at the same time. Removing the tilt removes these seasonal differences in the circular-orbit model.
limits: Circular orbit isolates tilt. Bodies are enlarged independently of orbital distance so the axis and daylight arcs can be inspected. Daily geometry is approximate and ignores refraction and weather.

title: The Moon has to turn
question: Would a Moon that never rotated always show us the same face?
explanation: To keep one marked face directed toward Earth, the Moon must turn once while travelling once around Earth. A Moon with no axial rotation would keep its marked direction fixed in space, so Earth would see different sides. Sunlight sets the illuminated half independently of that face marker.
limits: Circular orbit with schematic sizes. Lunar libration is omitted; this is not a dated Moon-rise calculator.

title: Find an eclipse by geometry
question: Why can a new Moon miss the Sun–Earth line?
explanation: Most new or full Moons pass above or below the Sun–Earth line because the lunar orbit is tilted. Near the two places where the orbital planes cross, the bodies can align and a shadow can intersect the target. The close-up shows the same calculated alignment and shadow boundaries as the overview.
limits: Circular orbits and fixed nodes; no dated ephemeris. Earth, Moon, orbital distance and shadow widths share one scale in 3D. The linked cut states its longitudinal and transverse scales; the optional central detail enlarges all transverse distances together.

title: Subtract Earth’s central pull
question: Why is there an outward relative pull on the far side?
explanation: The Moon pulls the near side more strongly than Earth’s centre and the far side less strongly. Relative to the falling centre, the near side accelerates toward the Moon while the far side falls behind. That far-side relative arrow points outward even though the Moon’s absolute pull is still inward.
limits: Ideal equilibrium tide pattern, with arrows hugely enlarged. Continents, ocean dynamics and Haji Ali timing are not predicted.

title: Count photons and electrons
question: Can bright red light beat the threshold by pooling its photons?
explanation: In this model one electron receives energy from one photon. Below the threshold, adding more photons does not give any one electron enough energy to escape. Above it, photon energy sets the maximum electron kinetic energy, while photon flux controls how many electrons can be emitted.
limits: Single-photon calcium model with work function 2.71 eV. A uniform 0-to-maximum electron-energy distribution is illustrative; multiphoton effects are outside this model.

title: An atom is mostly space
question: If a nucleus were a 1 cm marble, how large would the atom be?
explanation: The chosen atom reference diameter is one hundred thousand times the nucleus diameter. A nucleus one centimetre across would therefore belong to an atom reference about one kilometre across. At a true common scale the nucleus is unresolved; the cloud outline is a probability-region symbol, not an orbit or a solid wall.
limits: Approximate 10^5 diameter ratio; a cloud outline is a probability-region symbol rather than a solid boundary.

title: Exposure, contamination and decay
question: Does switching off a beam remove radioactive dust?
explanation: An external beam stops exposing the object when its source is switched off. Radioactive dust is different: the emitting atoms remain on the surface until removed or decayed. Each nucleus has a random decay time, while many nuclei together approach the smooth exponential expectation.
limits: Simulated decay events; half-life is chosen in arbitrary model seconds. No dose or biological-effect calculation.

title: From the solar core to light
question: Does the Sun’s light come from chemical burning at its surface?
explanation: Fusion in the hot core combines hydrogen into helium and releases energy corresponding to the reduction in total rest mass. Neutrinos carry some energy straight out; most heats the Sun and is transported through the radiative and convective layers before escaping as light. The visible transport sequence is schematic, not a measured travel-time simulation.
limits: Net reaction and atomic masses are bookkeeping. Transport is a schematic stage sequence, not a simulated photon diffusion time.

title: A halo around L1
question: Is L1 a place where gravity is zero?
explanation: The Sun’s pull and Earth’s opposing pull do not cancel at L1. Their remaining inward acceleration is what a craft needs to follow Earth’s yearly orbital motion. The linked projections show one schematic three-dimensional path near that balance region; they are not a mission forecast.
limits: Point masses for the force account; its distance control does not relocate the independently schematic 177.86-day halo. No mission ephemeris or integrated restricted-three-body orbit.

title: Same hydrogen, different lines
question: Does a weak hydrogen line mean little hydrogen?
explanation: In cool hydrogen few electrons occupy the excited level needed for strong Balmer absorption. At very high temperature much hydrogen is ionised, again leaving few electrons in that level. Stronger lines at an intermediate temperature therefore need not mean more hydrogen; compare temperature first, then abundance.
limits: LTE Saha–Boltzmann population proxy at fixed electron density 10^20 m^-3, ground-state partition approximation. Line depths are illustrative, not an atmosphere fit.

title: From a blink to a distance
question: Can a star look faint because it is distant rather than weak?
explanation: Parallax compares a known baseline with a tiny apparent shift. For a Cepheid, a calibrated relation between pulse period and luminosity estimates how bright the star really is. Comparing that luminosity with the received mean flux gives distance through the inverse-square relation; the pulse and graph share one clock.
limits: Triangle uses logarithmic distance and exaggerated angles; numerical parallax is physical. Cepheid relation and icon radius/colour are illustrative; extinction, metallicity and calibration uncertainty omitted.

title: More mass, smaller dwarf
question: Does adding material always make a star bigger?
explanation: No two electrons can occupy the same complete quantum state. Compression fills higher-momentum states, creating pressure even when the gas is cold. More mass means stronger gravity and a smaller supported radius; at the limiting mass this ideal stable model fails rather than producing a real zero-size star.
limits: Zero-temperature ideal relation with 1.44-solar-mass limiting mass. Zero radius marks model breakdown, not a physical white dwarf of zero size.

title: Choose another galaxy
question: If every distant galaxy recedes, are we at the centre?
explanation: Multiplying every separation by the same factor increases a larger separation by a larger amount. Any chosen galaxy therefore finds the same distance–recession relation when measuring relative positions. Individual bound galaxies keep their sizes while the gaps expand in this model.
limits: Homogeneous low-redshift Hubble-flow model; local peculiar velocities and general-relativistic light propagation are omitted.

title: A pendulum and a turning Earth
question: Would a Foucault pendulum precess equally in Mumbai and at the equator?
explanation: At a pole, Earth turns the floor beneath the swing through one full rotation per sidereal day. At lower latitude only the component of Earth’s rotation along the local vertical contributes to the slow turning of the swing direction relative to the floor. That component vanishes at the equator.
limits: Small-amplitude ideal pendulum; precession is the local approximation, not a claim of one globally fixed swing plane at every latitude.

title: An axle parallel to Earth’s
question: Why does Ooty’s latitude match the telescope’s slope?
explanation: An axle parallel to Earth’s rotation axis lets a telescope compensate for Earth’s turn by rotating about that one axis. Its elevation above a level horizon equals the observatory’s latitude. Mesh openings much smaller than the wavelength can act approximately like a continuous conductor; that size comparison is qualitative here.
limits: Equatorial-mount geometry is exact; mesh reflection is a qualitative wavelength comparison, not an electromagnetic solver.

title: Read a track through emulsion
question: Can a flat microscope image hide motion through the plate?
explanation: At a known momentum, a heavier charged particle moves more slowly and has a larger scattering and ionisation proxy in this model. Emulsion grains record a track, but a flat projection hides its depth. Finite microscope resolution broadens the conditional mass and speed interval rather than uniquely identifying the particle.
limits: Highland x/X₀=.01 proxy, 1/β² grain-density proxy; transverse magnification and resolution are labelled. Interval conditions on known momentum/material and omits energy loss and sampling uncertainty. This does not reconstruct historical plates.

title: Nature and its mirror
question: Does a mirror image of the weak-decay pattern remain an allowed pattern?
explanation: The electrons are emitted more often on one side of the aligned nuclear spins. A mirror transforms a spin arrow, defined by a right-hand rule, differently from an ordinary motion arrow. The mirrored picture reverses their correlation; weak decay favours one correlation rather than treating its mirror as equivalent.
limits: Illustrative angular asymmetry parameter 0.8, not historical count data. Nuclear spin is an arrow, not a classical spinning ball.

title: Count states, not labels
question: Does exchanging two identical photons produce a new state?
explanation: Swapping the named particles A and B changes a labelled arrangement. Swapping identical bosons leaves the observable occupation unchanged, so it must not be counted again. Identical same-spin fermions cannot share one one-particle state; the available-state and energy assumptions remain fixed here.
limits: Fixed two particles, two available one-particle states; no fixed-total-energy constraint. Counts alone do not assign general probabilities or derive Planck’s law.

title: Measure a tiny displaced star
question: Does one noisy measurement prove a theory?
explanation: An uncertainty interval shows the range allowed by the measurement’s finite precision. If two predictions both lie inside it, this measurement cannot distinguish them. Reducing the uncertainty may exclude a prediction, but agreement with one result alone does not prove a theory.
limits: Solar-limb general-relativistic deflection 1.75 arcseconds, scaled by inverse impact parameter. The plot is simulated evidence, not the 1919 plates. The 3D ray bend is enlarged for inspection; use the labelled arcsecond plot for measurement.
